title: Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis and Active Transport
description: Movement of substances in and out of cells, plus surface area to volume ratio for the challenges of size.
hero_image_caption: Root hair cells extend thread-like projections into the surrounding soil — a masterclass in biological surface-area engineering, maximising the uptake of water and mineral ions by osmosis and active transport.
content_html:
Moving Substances Into and Out of Cells

Cells need to transport substances across their membranes to survive. There are three main mechanisms: diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration — it is passive (no energy needed). Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out. The steeper the concentration gradient, the faster the rate of diffusion. Temperature and surface area also affect the rate — higher temperature means faster-moving particles and more frequent collisions.

Osmosis is specifically the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential). Osmosis is a special case of diffusion — only water molecules move, driven by the difference in water potential across the membrane. No energy is required.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy from respiration. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, where the concentration of minerals is lower than inside the cell. The energy comes from ATP produced by mitochondria in the root hair cells.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive processes (no energy needed, move down the concentration gradient). Active transport requires energy from respiration to move substances against the concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.

The classic osmosis practical uses potato cylinders placed in solutions of different sucrose concentrations. Cut cylinders of equal mass and length. Place one in distilled water, one in a low-concentration sucrose solution, one in a high-concentration sucrose solution. Leave for a set time (e.g. 30 minutes), remove, blot dry, and reweigh or remeasure.

In distilled water, water moves into the potato by osmosis (water potential of the potato cells is lower than the surrounding water), so the cylinder gains mass and becomes turgid. In a high-concentration sucrose solution, water moves out of the potato by osmosis (water potential of the sucrose solution is lower than the cells), so the cylinder loses mass and becomes flaccid or plasmolysed.

Plot a graph of percentage change in mass (y-axis) against sucrose concentration (x-axis). The intercept with the x-axis shows the isotonic point — where the water potential of the solution equals the water potential of the potato cells, so no net movement of water occurs.

A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 5.0 g. After being placed in distilled water for 30 minutes, its mass is 5.8 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.

Percentage change = \(\dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{original mass}} \times 100\) = \(\dfrac{5.8 - 5.0}{5.0} \times 100\) = \(\dfrac{0.8}{5.0} \times 100\) = +16%

A positive value means mass increased (water moved in by osmosis). A negative value would mean mass decreased (water moved out). Using percentage change rather than raw change in mass allows fair comparison between cylinders that had slightly different starting masses.

The Challenges of Size — Surface Area to Volume Ratio

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) decreases. Consider a cube: a 1 cm cube has SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, SA:V = 6:1. A 2 cm cube has SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³, SA:V = 3:1. This means simple diffusion alone cannot supply enough substances or remove waste fast enough for large organisms. Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

For a cube with side length l: SA = 6l², V = l³, SA:V ratio = 6l² ÷ l³ = 6/l.

Example: Calculate the SA:V ratio for cubes with sides 1 cm, 2 cm, and 4 cm:
1 cm cube: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, ratio = 6:1
2 cm cube: SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³, ratio = 3:1
4 cm cube: SA = 96 cm², V = 64 cm³, ratio = 1.5:1
As size doubles, SA:V ratio halves — larger organisms have a proportionally smaller surface area relative to their volume.

This is why a mouse loses body heat proportionally faster than an elephant — the mouse has a much higher SA:V ratio, so heat escapes more quickly relative to its body volume. It is also why single-celled organisms like amoeba can rely entirely on diffusion, while humans need a circulatory system.

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This is why multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. alveoli in lungs, villi in the intestine) and transport systems to move substances efficiently. Single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion because their SA:V ratio is high.

Specialised Exchange Surfaces

Large multicellular organisms have evolved specialised exchange surfaces to overcome the limitations of a low SA:V ratio. These surfaces share common features: large surface area (to maximise the rate of exchange), thin walls (to minimise diffusion distance), good blood/fluid supply (to maintain steep concentration gradients), and in some cases ventilation (to maintain fresh supply of gases).

Alveoli in the lungs have a very large total surface area, walls just one cell thick, and a dense capillary network — all adaptations that maximise gas exchange. Villi in the small intestine have microvilli on their surface (brush border), increasing the surface area still further for absorption of digested food molecules into the blood.

Root hair cells in plants have long, thin extensions that greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport from the soil. They contain many mitochondria to supply the ATP needed for active transport.
exam_tip_html: For osmosis questions, always use the correct term 'partially permeable membrane' and state the direction of water movement — from high water potential (dilute) to low water potential (concentrated). For SA:V ratio calculations, calculate surface area (all faces) and volume separately before dividing. A very common error is using raw change in mass rather than percentage change when comparing osmosis results across cylinders.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diffusion: passive movement of particles down a concentration gradient (no energy). Osmosis: passive movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from high to low water potential (no energy). Active transport: movement against the concentration gradient, requires ATP from respiration.
  • As organisms get larger, SA:V ratio decreases — making diffusion alone insufficient. Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi, root hairs) and transport systems.
  • Percentage change in mass = (change in mass ÷ original mass) × 100. SA:V ratio for a cube of side l = 6/l. Both are common calculation questions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following processes requires energy from respiration?
A) Diffusion
B) Osmosis
C) Active transport
D) All of the above
State the direction of water movement during osmosis.
practice_questions.marks: Water moves from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable membrane. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student could investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on potato cylinders using osmosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for any two of the following:
• Cut potato cylinders of equal size/mass and place each in a different concentration of sucrose solution (1)
• Leave for a set time, blot dry, and measure the change in mass (or length) (1)
• Calculate the percentage change in mass to allow fair comparison (1)
• Repeat to improve reliability / calculate a mean (1)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a single-celled organism such as an amoeba can obtain enough oxygen by diffusion alone, but a mammal cannot.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• A single-celled organism is very small and has a high surface area to volume ratio (1)
• This means diffusion distance to the centre of the cell is short and the rate of diffusion is sufficient to meet the cell's needs (1)
• A mammal is much larger and has a low SA:V ratio — diffusion alone cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to all cells deep inside the organism, so specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. lungs/alveoli) and a circulatory system are needed (1)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 4.0 g. After 30 minutes in a sucrose solution, its mass is 3.4 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass and state whether water entered or left the cell. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ original mass) × 100 (1)
Change in mass = 3.4 − 4.0 = −0.6 g (1)
Percentage change = (−0.6 ÷ 4.0) × 100 = −15% (1)
Mass decreased, so water left the cell by osmosis — the sucrose solution had a lower water potential than the potato cells (1)
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells are well adapted for the absorption of water and mineral ions from the soil.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• Root hair cells have long, thin extensions that greatly increase the surface area in contact with the soil (1)
• This maximises the rate of absorption by providing more membrane for water and ions to cross (1)
• Water moves into root hair cells by osmosis — from the high water potential of the soil water to the lower water potential inside the cell, through the partially permeable membrane (1)
• Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport against the concentration gradient (1)
• Root hair cells contain many mitochondria to supply the ATP needed for active transport (1)
• The thin cell wall and membrane minimise the diffusion distance for water molecules (1)

StudyVault Mastering: all six points covered with osmosis and active transport distinguished clearly, and SA:V and mitochondria adaptations both named.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes osmosis?
options: Movement of any dissolved substance from high to low concentration
Movement of water molecules from high to low water potential through a partially permeable membrane
Movement of substances against the concentration gradient using energy
Movement of oxygen into cells during respiration

knowledge_checks.q: A cube has sides of length 3 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
Why do root hair cells contain many mitochondria: _____
options: To provide ATP for active transport of mineral ions
To increase the surface area for diffusion
To store excess glucose as starch
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is To provide ATP for active transport of mineral ions.

knowledge_checks.q: A potato cylinder gains mass when placed in distilled water. This is because ___.: _____
options: Mineral ions diffuse into the potato
Water moves into the potato by osmosis down the water potential gradient
Active transport moves glucose into the potato
Enzymes break down the sucrose in the water
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is Water moves into the potato by osmosis down the water potential gradient.

knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down the concentration gradient. It is passive — no energy is required.
The net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable.

flashcard_questions.q: What is active transport and why does it require energy?
flashcard_questions.a: The movement of substances against the concentration gradient (from low to high concentration), requiring energy (ATP) from respiration. Example: root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from the soil.

flashcard_questions.q: How does surface area to volume ratio change as an organism gets larger?
flashcard_questions.a: It decreases — as size increases, volume grows faster than surface area. This is why larger organisms need transport systems: diffusion alone is too slow to supply all cells.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you calculate percentage change in mass for an osmosis experiment?
flashcard_questions.a: Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ original mass) × 100. Use percentage change (not raw mass change) to allow fair comparisons between cylinders.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to a plant cell placed in a concentrated sucrose solution?
flashcard_questions.a: Water leaves the cell by osmosis (toward the lower water potential of the sucrose), causing the cell to become flaccid.

flashcard_questions.q: Calculate the SA:V ratio for a 5 cm cube.
flashcard_questions.a: Surface area = 6 × 5² = 150 cm². Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³. SA:V ratio = 150:125 = 1.2:1 (or 6/5 = 1.2).

glossary_terms.definition: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient.
The net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential) through a partially permeable membrane.
The movement of substances from a lower concentration to a higher concentration against the concentration gradient, requiring energy from respiration.
The difference in concentration of a substance between two areas. A steeper gradient means faster diffusion.
A membrane that allows some molecules (like water) to pass through but blocks larger molecules.
The ratio of an organism's surface area to its volume. As organisms get larger, this ratio decreases, making diffusion alone insufficient for supplying all cells.
